what.formal: Recap of the object the whole section builds. A **decision tree** routes an input through tests of the form $x_j \le t$ (numeric) or $x_j \in S$ (categorical), one test per internal node, and returns the prediction stored at the leaf reached — the majority class for a classification leaf, the mean of the training targets for a regression leaf. It is grown by greedily choosing, at each node, the candidate split that most reduces the node's **impurity**: entropy $H = -\sum_k p_k\log_2 p_k$ for ID3, the gain ratio $\mathrm{IG}/\mathrm{SplitInfo}$ for C4.5, and Gini impurity $1 - \sum_k p_k^2$ with the squared-error criterion for CART. It is then cut back by pruning, because a tree grown to purity has zero training error on any dataset.
what.plain: A tree is a flowchart of threshold tests ending in leaves that hold answers, built by repeatedly taking the question that separates the labels best, and then trimmed so it stops fitting the noise.

what.md: This section taught eight things. If you can do all of them unaided, skip ahead — the boosting section assumes this material and does not repeat it.

items: State what a decision tree is, and extract the if-then rule list and the feature-space partition from a drawn tree.
Say what impurity means, and name the three classical measures with their formulas: entropy and information gain for ID3, gain ratio for C4.5, Gini impurity for CART.
Compute the entropy of a node from its class counts, and compute the information gain of a candidate split, including the size weighting of the children.
Explain why information gain is biased towards features with many distinct values, and how dividing by SplitInfo repairs it — and how it fails to repair it completely.
Explain what a numeric feature's threshold candidates are, and why there are one fewer of them than there are distinct values.
Compute a CART split: Gini impurity and its gain for classification, squared-error reduction for regression.
Explain why an unpruned tree reaches zero training error, and compare pre-pruning with post-pruning, including what cost-complexity pruning minimises.
Name the four limits of a tree — overfitting, axis-parallel boundaries, no extrapolation, instability — and say which of them an ensemble does and does not remove.

what.md: The questions below are the check. Two of the four correct is not the bar — the bar is that you did not have to think hard about any of them. If you hesitated on the split arithmetic, stay: the boosting section fits each new tree to the errors the previous trees left behind, and it assumes you can already evaluate a criterion and read a leaf.

example.md: **One recap, end to end.** Four rows, two features, and the whole procedure from entropy to a decision. This is the shortest complete run of the machinery in this section.

Parent: 3 rows labelled Yes and 1 labelled No, so the proportions are $0.75$ and $0.25$. Entropy $= -0.75\log_2 0.75 - 0.25\log_2 0.25 = 0.3113 + 0.5000 = 0.8113$ bits. Gini $= 1 - (0.75^2 + 0.25^2) = 1 - 0.625 = 0.375$.

Candidate Size. Big holds rows 1 and 2, both Yes: entropy 0, weight $2/4$. Small holds rows 3 and 4, one No and one Yes: entropy 1.0000, weight $2/4$. Weighted $= (0.5)(0) + (0.5)(1.0000) = 0.5000$, so the gain is $0.8113 - 0.5000 = 0.3113$ bits. By Gini: Big gives $1 - (1^2 + 0^2) = 0$; Small gives $1 - (0.5^2 + 0.5^2) = 0.5$; weighted $= 0.2500$; Gini gain $= 0.375 - 0.2500 = 0.1250$.

Candidate Colour. Red holds rows 1, 3, 4, labels Yes, No, Yes: proportions $0.6667$ and $0.3333$, entropy $0.9183$, weight $3/4$. Blue holds row 2 only, Yes: entropy 0, weight $1/4$. Weighted $= (0.75)(0.9183) + (0.25)(0) = 0.6887$, so the gain is $0.8113 - 0.6887 = 0.1226$ bits. By Gini: Red gives $1 - (0.4444 + 0.1111) = 0.4444$; Blue gives 0; weighted $= (0.75)(0.4444) = 0.3333$; Gini gain $= 0.375 - 0.3333 = 0.0417$.

Both criteria prefer Size, and both prefer it by a comfortable margin: 0.3113 against 0.1226 by entropy, 0.1250 against 0.0417 by Gini. The tree's root test is Size. Note that the two criteria report different numbers for the same split and agree on the ranking, which is the expected behaviour and the reason either can be used; note also that the Colour split sends only one row to its Blue branch, which is the structural signature of a feature that will not generalise and the kind of case gain ratio was built to notice.

**Reading the whole section off this one example.** The parent entropy is the budget; the weighted child entropy is the cost; the difference is the score; the largest score picks the question. Everything in cards 2 to 5 is a variation on those four lines, and everything in cards 6 and 7 is about what happens to the tree after it has been grown this way.

quiz.q: Which pairing of criterion with algorithm is correct?

opts.md: Gini impurity is ID3's criterion; information gain is CART's
opts.expl: This reverses the two. Both are impurity-gain criteria with the same shape, which is exactly why the names get swapped; the distinguishing features are that ID3's measure has a logarithm and CART's does not.

opts.md: Information gain is ID3's; gain ratio is C4.5's; Gini impurity is CART's
opts.expl: Correct. The three form a sequence of repairs: ID3 splits on gain, C4.5 divides that gain by SplitInfo to penalise finely cutting tests, and CART replaces the whole measure with Gini, which needs no logarithm, and adds binary-only splits and cost-complexity pruning.

opts.md: All three use entropy, and the only difference is how they handle numeric features
opts.expl: Only ID3 and C4.5 use entropy. CART uses Gini for classification and squared error for regression, neither of which involves a logarithm — that absence is one of the reasons CART is the base learner inside boosting libraries.

quiz.q: A node contains 9 rows: 6 labelled A and 3 labelled B. Compute its Gini impurity.
quiz.hint: Square each class proportion, add the squares, subtract from 1. Note that the proportions are two thirds and one third.
quiz.sol: The proportions are p_A = 6/9 = 0.6667 and p_B = 3/9 = 0.3333. Squaring: 0.4444 and 0.1111. Sum: 0.5556. Gini impurity = 1 - 0.5556 = 0.4444. As a check against the two anchors: a 9-to-0 node would give 1 - 1 = 0, and a node with equal classes would give 0.5; 0.4444 sits between them, closer to the balanced end, which is consistent with a two-to-one split.

quiz.q: A team must forecast a monthly revenue series that has grown steadily for four years, then fit the same pipeline to a churn-prediction table. Which statement is correct?

opts.md: The tree will serve both tasks equally, since the criterion is chosen from the data rather than by the user
opts.expl: The criterion is chosen by the algorithm, but the model class is chosen by the user, and the model class is what decides whether the task is possible. This is a case where the choice of model class, not the choice of criterion, is the whole story.

opts.md: The churn table is a normal case for a tree; the revenue series is not, because a tree predicts a leaf mean and so cannot forecast a value above the largest target it trained on
opts.expl: Correct. Revenue that grows means the future lies outside the training range, and a tree's output is capped by the training target range because every leaf returns a mean of training targets and every leaf region is unbounded. The forecast would be flat at the average level of the last training window. The fix is to give the tree the trend rather than to ask it to invent one: difference the series, or model the trend separately and predict the residual with the tree. Churn, by contrast, is a binary label with no ordering, so the leaf-mean cap is irrelevant.

opts.md: Neither task works, because trees cannot handle numeric targets at all
opts.expl: Regression trees are part of CART and are the form used in boosting; the rectangle criterion of card 5 is defined for numeric targets. The limit is extrapolation, not numeric targets.

quiz.q: In card 3's six-row dataset, changing one label out of six changed the root test from Outlook to Wind. Which conclusion follows?

opts.md: The information gain criterion is incorrect, since a correct criterion would not change its answer
opts.expl: The criterion computed exactly what it is defined to compute, and the two gains it compared were 0.4591 and 0.0817 before the change and 0.0441 and 0.4591 after. The reversal is a fact about the data, not an arithmetic error.

opts.md: The tree structure is unstable with respect to the training data, which is a real limitation of a single tree and a reason an ensemble that averages many trees performs better
opts.expl: Correct. Six rows is an extreme case, but the effect does not vanish on larger tables — it shrinks. Instability is the one failure mode on card 7's list that ensembling genuinely removes, because averaging many trees fitted to slightly different versions of the data cancels the part of the structure that was arbitrary. This is also why a single tree's variable-importance ranking should not be read as a stable statement about the data.

opts.md: The dataset is too small to fit any model, so no conclusion about trees in general follows
opts.expl: Size explains how dramatic the flip was, not why it happened. The mechanism — two candidate scores close enough that a small perturbation reverses their order — is present in every dataset, and the standard response is to average over resamples, which is exactly the ensemble remedy.

close: **You are ready for the ensemble.** The next section adds trees together one at a time, each fitted to what the previous ones got wrong. Everything it assumes about a single tree — its criterion, its regression form, its failure modes — is on this card's list.
